subject: Cognitive Science
title: Treisman's Attenuation Model
description: A fast breakdown of Treisman's Attenuation Model for builders.

hook.text: If the filter blocks everything, how does your name slip through at a party? Anne Treisman had an answer.

buildup.text: She proposed that unattended signals aren't blocked—they're turned down, like lowering a volume knob.

discovery.text: Important signals like your name have a low activation threshold. Even a whisper triggers them.

twist.text: This means the brain processes unattended input partially—not fully, but not zero either.

climax.text: Treisman's model explained what Broadbent's couldn't: a flexible gate, not a brick wall.

quiz.question: What did Treisman say happens to unattended messages?

details.summary: Anne Treisman modified Broadbent's theory by proposing that unattended information is not blocked but attenuated, or turned down like a volume dial. Important signals like your name have a low activation threshold and can still break through even when the channel is dimmed.
details.whyItMatters: Treisman's model elegantly explained cocktail party effects while preserving the idea of a filter. It showed that attention operates on a continuum rather than as an all-or-nothing gate.
takeaways: Treisman proposed attenuation rather than complete blocking
Important stimuli have low thresholds and can break through
The model bridges early and late selection theories

faq.question: How does attenuation differ from complete filtering?
faq.answer: Complete filtering blocks all unattended input. Attenuation reduces the signal strength but does not eliminate it. If the weakened signal matches a low-threshold detector like your own name, it still reaches awareness. This explains breakthrough effects.

faq.question: What evidence supports the attenuation model?
faq.answer: Studies show people detect their own name in unattended channels about one-third of the time. Bilingual speakers notice translations of attended words in unattended channels. These findings fit attenuation better than complete blockage.
